item.title: The Dividual Strikes Back
item.description:
why nothing and everything is your fault

Quick note: If you’d prefer to listen to this, I read it aloud here.

In Vincenzo Natali’s 1997 cult indie classic film “Cube” a group of disconnected individuals awake alone in a labyrinth of identical interlocking rooms. Throughout the film they must find each other and work together to survive a ghastly array of fatal traps and puzzle their way out. Each character seems to have a purpose; a doctor, a police officer, an escape artist, a maths wiz and we see them coordinate their unique skills to outwit the sadistic mastermind behind…

… The Cube

It’s a film about our human capacity for cooperation, the benefits and the difficulties, but the genius of the film—the evil genius—spoiler alert: is that the villain is also human cooperation. We find out that Worth; a character whose worth to the group appears to be to make unhelpful jaded jibes at every turn, turns out to be an engineer responsible for designing a component of the Cube, with no idea what the whole was.

I never even left my office, I talked on the phone to some people, specialists, other guys like me, working on small details, no one knew what it was…

The Cube turns out to be an invention of no one in particular, but rather the product of the siloed alignment between specialists just following orders. The project gets completed because that’s what projects must do, the product gets used because that’s what products must do.

This may be hard for you to understand, but there’s no conspiracy, nobody is in charge. It’s a headless blunder operating under the illusion of a master plan.

The Dividual

In a previous post, The Era of the Dividual, I used this archaic term to refer to entities that can be seen to function in the world through individuals, but independently of them. The first is Milton’s conception of proscribed religion, where a religious person must adhere to dogma imposed from the outside, rather than from an internal sense of what is true. Another example was social media algorithms, that dictate viral success independent from the star-power of an individual, and then finally we looked at the presidency of Donald Trump as an example of an individual entity with so little integrity or consistency, that he is able to politically shape-shift.

A Particular Type of Siloed Alignment

In “Cube” the dividual is the “headless blunder” born of the cooperative actions of individuals, without any overall design or “conspiracy”, there is no individual mastermind. This comes as a result of a very particular type of siloed alignment, where, because individual specialists are kept separate from each other and importantly from “the head”, they end up complicit in creating a product no one wants.

The idea of self-interested individuals being complicit in their collective destruction might sound familiar to some readers, because it’s the exact description of a character we’ve dealt with here on the blog, the antagonist, humanity’s nemesis, the god of negative sum games…

Moloch

A perfect example of a “dividual” is Moloch, an entity that exists outside any one individual, but is so clearly identifiable by its behaviour, that it seems to have its own motivations and personality—the cube is a perfect manifestation of Moloch.

We increasingly exist in a system where we are contributing at all times to work projects, markets, information eco-systems, financial systems and political systems with increasing anonymity, and decreasing exposure to direct feedback. The accountability that is inherent in face-to-face interactions is dissolving as we become dividual.

The Good Place

The result is that we are complicit in everything from environmental degradation to modern slavery, a point made well in The Good Place where Ted Danson’s character explains that the “points system” for getting into “The Good Place” no longer works, because the world is simply too interconnected, it is impossible not to be a small part of many globally significant crimes with every minor choice we make.

But at the same time, our involvement is so diffuse that no one could reasonably point at any one person and say “you’re responsible for this.” and so great evils are able to continue.

Just Following Orders

I learned of this dynamic playing out in a deliberate way when I visited the Nazi work camp Sachsenhausen. On this dark tour, we were guided by a young Masters student studying German history. He took us to Station Z, and explained how the victim would go through a series of stages, involving different officers before execution. Each officer had a specific role; checking identification, weighing and health checks, in some cases photography. The conceit of these checks was to disguise the execution as a fitness assessment to prevent resistance, but it served the dual purpose of distributing (and therefore diluting) the sense of responsibility for the execution. Eventually it was one officer’s job to align the victim’s head with a hole in the wall, and stand aside, the final trigger was pulled by an SS officer in another room who could not see and did not know anything about the victim they were shooting through the hole.

The whole process was intended to create the “banality” in what Hannah Arendt famously termed “the banality of evil”.

What About Us?

I give this example because I think it’s important to recognise the lengths the Nazi leadership had to go through to othervictims in order to bypass human instincts. Siloed alignment gives us great power without requisite accountability. It makes me question what systems we have at present that utilise similar mechanisms, whether designed intentionally, like with the Nazis, or blundered into like in “Cube”.

This othering of the victim is still the end result of this particular type of siloed alignment. The accidental and designed mechanisms for siloing cooperators from each other that we’ve discussed, contribute to a wider siloing of a strongly aligned group; “the cooperators” against another group; “the other”.

Meaty Misdirection

A glaring example personally is factory farming—and my own complicity in it. I am not a vegan, or even a vegetarian, and while I endeavour to buy free-range meat and eggs, I am not as vigilant as I could be. The meat industry, by design and by an accident of the division of labour, involves a vast cooperative network of largely siloed stages, from factories, which have their own Station Z-like processes for eliminating resistance from livestock and staff, to packaging, to marketing, to distribution. The process of eating meat is very much divorced, by the time it reaches the consumer, from the process of killing and preparing the meat.

The process of siloed alignment undergone makes eating the meat infinitely more (morally) palatable for the consumer, because the animal being killed has been successfully othered.

So…

We are perhaps all unwittingly horsemen in the gathering apocalypse—how do we get ourselves out of this mess? Have we been here before? Can we learn anything from other existential threats we’ve survived in the past. Next up we take a look at one of the strangest and most consequential standoffs in history, the nuclear standoff, otherwise known as MAD.

item.title: The Missing Product Layers in AI Safety
item.description:
Epistemic Status: We’re highly confident in how the larger tech industry defines roles, makes decisions and builds products based on our years of experience in it. We’re fairly confident in the frontier labs operational models based on their job postings. Our suggestions for what to build and how to have gone through some pressure testing, and confidence could be raised through discussion with leaders in AI Safety to further understand what makes this space unique.

Intro

Frontier labs have adopted proven methodologies from tech to build their capabilities using matrixed organizations, including builders. This allows them to advance at a rapid pace, keeping their flywheel spinning, while AI safety struggles to keep up.

To prevent serious risks of advanced AI, AI safety needs to close that gap and one way to accomplish that is by building products that address common needs and diffuse AI safety outputs to compound their impact. There are aligned people that have extensive experience building products, but are not currently finding opportunities in existing organizations or through founder support to build them.

We (the authors and collaborators) each have 10+ years of experience at successful tech startups and in big tech. At EAGxBerkeley, we compared notes on gaps we were observing, our hypotheses on addressing them and wanted to share our perspectives with the broader community.

We’re writing this post to generate awareness, discussion, and ideally to open up discussion with safety leaders, fieldbuilders and funders on how to start building.

Background

An AI safety output spans research, controls, defenses, governance, policy and more. The pace of outputs being generated continues to increase, but there is limited work to connect them back up the chain to the highest level impact of avoiding serious risks to humans. These outputs accumulate in a patchwork of papers, forum posts, blogs, GitHub repositories and more where they rely on a highly-engaged community to continuously discover, consume and adopt. It assumes that the best ideas will win out and gain traction, but provides no formal pathway to achieve that.

We observe a field primarily organized as many small research teams producing many small, loosely coupled artifacts, but lacking layers above those efforts to bring the outputs back together so that they can be quickly applied and adopted by the broader community. For example in the evals tooling landscape Inspect and Petri exist as frameworks but no layer sits above them to standardize the techniques, processes, data and connect all phases of evaluations to ensure that trustworthy results and reporting are generated.

Coefficient Giving’s Fall 2026 Project Tailwind highlights this in multiple areas, such as this challenge statement for their proposed AI uplift for AI Safety initiative:

“There is a coordination failure here: investing in tools and best practices for using AI to accelerate AI safety and governance is a public good that individual contributors often lack capacity for. The individuals already doing this work have limited resources and can’t serve the entire field.”

Threat model

We believe that AI is not normal technology and poses serious risks to humans during both development and deployment across misalignment, misuse, loss of control, and systemic and structural harm. Across all these vectors products and tools play a role in harm reduction (in addition to research and governance). There is awareness of the importance of products [goodgravy 2022, Hobbhahn 2026] and tools [Jones 2021, BlueDot 2025], yet broadly AI safety doesn’t clearly differentiate between the two currently, nor does it robustly support creating products.

Examples of gaps observed in AI safety products and tools

Below is a limited sample of the types of needs we’ve observed across AI safety with concrete references.

Risk vector and Jobs to Be Done

Exists

Missing

Misalignment: know when a model has the wrong objective and why

Products: Neuronpedia


Tools: Petri, Bloom, TransformerLens 

Access to frontier models beyond black-box [Casper 2024]



Misuse: know when a model is being used for harmful purposes, and if a deployment can be jailbroken

Products: per-deployer app-layer solutions (Lakera, Giskard)


Tools: Inspect Evals dangerous capabilities



Shared frontier uplift evals (vs bespoke ones from AISI, METR)

Loss of control: detect and stop autonomous scheming or sabotage

Products: Apollo Watcher (monitor for coding agents); agent tracing in Weave and 
Braintrust; runtime guardrails e.g. Lakera Guard, which cover prompt injection, not control.


Tools: ControlTower (Redwood, Equistamp, Luthien), Inspect Sentinel, Luthien-Proxy, ControlArena (UKAISI)

Shared autonomy evals.


Shared protocol results.


An agreed stop mechanism.


Limited benchmark coverage for evade-oversight, self-replication, and AI R&D (Bench-2-CoP 2025)

Systemic and structural: know what is trending towards failure and disempowerment

Almost nothing specific. The nearest instruments are cross-cutting capability trends and incidents.

Measurement for concentration of power, epistemic harm, multi-agent effects

Across all four risk vectors

Products: Docent, Epoch hub for capability trends, AI Incident Database for failures.


Tools: eval framework (Inspect)

Widespread safe access layers (e.g. OpenMined)


Standardized reports for policymakers with actionable insights.


Standard elicitation, so two evaluators with the same access get the same result


A full harness to monitor and reproduce a failure (logging, reconstruct, re-run)

How to Build Products that Compound AI Safety’s Impact

While the idea of a product and related roles stretches back decades, it really began to coalesce in the 2000s and saw broad adoption in the 2010s. Although it continues to evolve as AI disrupts our ways of working, the principles remain the primary structure of how big tech and the frontier labs operate at scale. This allows them to rapidly pivot to whatever will deliver the most value by focusing on deeply understanding their users needs through user research and objective metrics that allow them to continuously learn and iterate while measuring themselves through outcomes over outputs.

Products vs tools

A product can be used by a wide range of people [Brooks 1975, chapter 1], without discussion with the creator, for a “job-to-be-done” (JTBD). These jobs are about achieving an outcome: “People don't want to buy a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole!” [Levitt 1969]. A product has customers: people who choose to adopt it and pay for it with their time (always) and their money (often). Products are complex to build and deliver, and require specific expertise. In the tech industry, a “product team” [Cagan 2019] refers to a cross-functional team with product managers and engineers, and often designers and data scientists / data engineers. A product often starts off as a tool: built for a narrow purpose, by and for a narrower group of people. A product has one accountable owner for whether it gets adopted [Cagan 2017] whereas a tool has maintainers. Tools (such as open source libraries) may be powerful but are typically provided with few or no guarantees of suitability, which hampers widespread adoption.

Theory of Change

Our proposal is that building a new layer of products that continuously build on those outputs and connect them to users wherever they are will lower the barrier to adoption and application, and thus support bending the curve of AI safety efforts to close the gap to frontier capabilities. We would observe this through near-term signals that show a correlation of this work and increasing the output rate while decreasing the effort per safety output. In the medium-term we expect the time to detect a novel harmful capability or propensity to decrease, while the trustworthiness and credibility of outputs bend upwards.

Impact

Avoid serious risks to humans during development and deployment of advanced AI across misalignment, misuse, loss of control, systemic and structural harm.

Goal

AI safety closes the gap to, and then keeps pace with frontier capabilities.

Inputs

A pipeline: of experienced builders from industry paired up with a corpus of existing but disconnected AI safety research, analysis, policy, tooling and infrastructure work. Orgs and funding that are bought into the need to scale and are comfortable supporting something currently undefined.

Outputs

Products: that solve common user needs built on top of existing tooling and infrastructure and alongside existing roles, by a newly defined builder role with prioritization authority and accountability to outcomes.

Primary Outcome
(⭐ the spine)

Applied & Adopted: AI safety outputs (research, controls, defenses, governance, policy and more) are broadly diffused across all functions, roles and orgs allowing widespread application and adoption. The field's output compounds instead of accumulating.

2nd Outcome

Shared Scaffolding: AI safety orgs operate at maximum effectiveness as they adopt common infrastructure, tooling and processes to be used internally.

3rd Outcome

Reproducible & Comparable: AI safety outputs become faster, more trustworthy, and ready to be reproduced and reused because shared tooling makes it easy to access and review everyone’s work.


Figure 1: Demonstration of bending AI safety curve to close and then bypass AI capabilities in support of alignment to reduce risks of harms.

Principles of building AI safety products

What we’ve observed independently, through conversations with those in AI safety, and through sources like Project Tailwind 2026 initiatives and Forethought’s Design sketches for a more sensible world is a through line of common principles. We think products should be built on principles like the ones below to maximize their adoption and usage:

  • Standardization: AI safety work and outputs are performed and captured consistently to create work that can be trusted and easily understood. Supports operational discipline, clear methodologies, calibrated reporting and excellent security. Examples: “...clear methodology, credible assessors (including potential subcontracts with existing third-party evaluators), calibrated reporting, and excellent internal security.” - Tailwind 2026: Independent AI auditors. “Maintain a recommended suite of best practices for measuring and promoting monitorability of frontier models” - Tailwind 2026: Oversight of CoT monitorability
  • Centralization: Setups, inputs, results, analyses, final outputs and more are stored centrally in a consistent way that makes it easy for anyone to access and reuse.  Examples: “That evidence is scattered across papers, blog posts, and Twitter threads, and the decision-makers who most need a clear view rarely have time to assemble it themselves.” - Tailwind 2026: State of AI Risk. “understanding the state of AI safety practices across different companies is difficult, and there’s no one canonical resource tracking and evaluating their safety practices” - Tailwind 2026: Frontier lab Accountability
  • Democratization: Support for anyone to set up, run and review any AI safety work. Supports task completion by lower-tier roles without direct intervention or oversight from domain experts. “Highly customised tools help individuals to understand themselves better and make decisions they endorse. We vastly uplift forecasting and scenario planning, massively improving our strategic awareness, and democratizing access to this kind of information.” - Forethought: Design Sketches for a More Sensible World. “Providing non-technical audiences – and policymakers, in particular – with clear, accurate, and compelling information about the frontiers of AI is critical for sound policymaking and regulation.” - Tailwind 2026: Frontier Capabilities Observatory.
  • Modularity and flexibility: Easily share, explore, try and adopt emerging AI safety capabilities. Allows rapid diffusion of new work across the space. Example: “Improving evals tooling is fairly architecture agnostic, or could be much more quickly adapted to future changes than it would take to build from scratch in the future.” - LessWrong: Hobbhahn 2026
  • End-to-End User Journeys: Create tools and solutions that span complete user journeys without the need to jump between or merge together multiple tools, datasets and codebases.  Examples: “A largely automated eval stack that is able to iteratively design, test, and improve evaluations” - LessWrong: Hobbhahn 2026 . “Given a question, the tool gathers relevant evidence, lays out the competing arguments, identifies the main points, and provides an overall assessment with a stated confidence level.” - Tailwind 2026: AI for decision-makers

Product Examples

  • Centralized storage of research, differential data and more - Make it easy for anyone or any product to access all relevant data and information in their domain of interest.
  • Policymaking Intelligence - Bridge the gaps between technical, bio, nuclear, cyber and other domains to policymakers, making it easy to stay up to date and make informed decisions.
  • Unified automated evals platform - Encourages consistent setups, analysis and outputs while supporting emerging techniques from research through a marketplace.
  • Unified controls platform - Makes it easy to design, stress-test and compare safety protocols and monitors for potentially misaligned AI agents, measuring the safety-usefulness tradeoff through consistent red-team vs. blue-team control evaluations.

Additionally, Ankur Pandey has generated a related sample list here as part of his AISafety.Builders fellowship.

How to Build Products

Modern products and the teams that build them largely operate off of a few standard operating principles and practices built upon Agile, with some highlights being:

  • Focus on the user - Deeply understand the user through user interviews, studying their feedback and objective measures, and ensure implementation meets their requirements.
  • Bias for action - Continuously deliver proofs of concept and then small improvements to working software over long research and implementation cycles.
  • Flexibility - Plans frequently change due to the above. Be willing to quickly pivot when something new emerges or something isn’t working out.
  • Measure outcomes over outputs - An output is simply creating something. Outcome is how you know the outputs delivered created the expected impact and value.
  • Matrixed roles - Most orgs feature multiple people working together representing their points of view to arrive at a solution that balances all the variables of delivering high quality workflows through scalable and maintainable code and infrastructure. More on this below.

Why Agile or Other Common Methodologies?

Given the existing gap to frontier capabilities, there is no time to reinvent the wheel while wasting time on ideas that are not panning out or delivering the largest impact.  These methodologies offer a standardized way to cut through noise and organize work to be efficient and highly effective.  They offer a set of principles and values, rather than a hard set of rules, although they have often gotten a bad reputation for being implemented as strict mandates.

While the exact implementation of these continue to evolve and vary org to org, overall big tech, startups and the frontier labs continue to employ them. Why? Because they're proven to help teams move faster and cheaper. Leading Agile consultant BCG estimates Agile can unlock 2-4x acceleration in time-to-market and new product delivery while also offering 15-25% reduction in development costs.  The 2025 State of Agile reported, “Focus is shifting to outcomes: Customer satisfaction (52%) remains the primary measure of success, followed by efficiency and cost reduction (40%).”

Who Builds Products

Anyone can build a product, regardless of their job title or function as long as they’re focused on delivering outcomes. An exceptionally broadly talented engineer or researcher may be able to cover all or most functional areas below. But, it’s often a lot of context to hold together, they don’t always have strengths in each area, and there is a lot of benefit in regular discussion among peers with diverse points of view.  This also differs from the generalist operational roles: the builders own the what, why and how and are often called to define that from vague open-ended problems.  Paul has written more about the builder role profile, its differentiation and a sample job description in Experienced Builders Role Profile and Job Descriptions.

These are some common roles used on teams developing products:

  • Product Managers - Represents the inputs from users, leadership and stakeholders.  Leads the feature prioritization process and is accountable to the agreed upon outcomes.
  • UX Designers - Often use design thinking, design sprints and rapid prototyping to quickly gather data on how users interact with systems, in order to improve their design. UX Researchers use human-computer interaction (for software systems) and the techniques described in The Design of Everyday Things (for anything including physical products) to understand the complex relationship between humans and products.
  • Engineers - Represents creating outputs that can be scaled and sustainable. Identifies the options that can solve user problems the fastest.
  • Scientists, Researchers & Analysts - Represents robust methods for getting the right answers from the data that they may also help pull or generate. Especially important for products that use AI and/or ML.

A note on role flattening in the age of AI: While it's true that product and researcher/analyst roles are changing, product and engineering are owning more design, etc, it's still important to have core roles that cover the full product development lifecycle including continuous improvement.  For example, engineering should still own ensuring the code implemented is robust, secure and ready to scale.  Analysts should validate feedback and metrics pulled by product or engineering that’s driving decisions, and product managers should guide how that data impacts feature prioritization.

Conclusion and Call to Action

We think there is a large set of challenges across the higher layers of AI safety that call for products to be built that would help close the gap to frontier capabilities. Further, we think that applying industry standard product practices and methodologies, and employing experienced builders from industry would allow them to be built faster, and more efficiently.

How to Support This

We’d like to hear from funders, fieldbuilders, organizational leaders, and any other leaders in AI safety that deeply understand the current state and plans to close the gap to frontier capabilities to discuss integrating experienced builders into the ecosystem to build products.

We propose AI Safety orgs take the following steps:

  • Field-builders should recruit experienced builders and help them build AI safety context and define potential products, then connect them to opportunities.
  • Organizations should hire candidates that help existing orgs adopt product best practices, invest in building products, and hire builders to accelerate their development.
  • Funders should support new organizations that build tools and products, especially if these don’t cleanly fit into an existing organization’s mission.

Appendix

References

A lot has already been written about generalists and mid-to-late career professionals entering AI safety. The below articles are some of what we built on top of as we were writing this article.

  • AI Safety's Biggest Talent Gap Isn't Researchers. It's Generalists. - Topaz - Effective Altruism Forum
  • I Want You for AI Safety - Sophie Kim - The Counterfactual
  • AI Safety Needs Mid-Career On-Ramps - Sophie Kim - Effective Altruism Forum
  • AI safety needs more operations professionals (Scaling organisations making AI go well) - Matt Beard - 80,000 Hours
  • Lateral Workshop Applications: A Case Study - Jacob Brinton, Seth Lifland - LessWrong
  • New talent is coming to AI safety. What happens next? - Enisa Ismaili - Effective Altruism Forum
  • Meta: The Job (Almost) Nobody Can Picture - Devon Fritz - Substack
  • The Grown-Ups Aren’t Coming (Philanthropic capital is coming faster than the infrastructure to absorb it, and infrastructure takes years to build. Please build it!) - Devon Fritz - Substack
  • The case for AGI safety products - Marius Hobbhahn - LessWrong
  • The Case for Building AI Safety Tools - Ankur Pandey - Substack

We'd like to thank Cibi Sounder and Hernan Barijhoff for reviewing this post as it evolved, as well as a handful of others that helped grow this idea and provide initial inputs, but didn't wish to be named.

item.title: Limiting Charging to 80%
item.description:
In an ideal world the incentives on phone manufacturers would be to optimize useful lifetime, but instead people buy phones based on their as-new performance. Which means phones charge to 100% even though that's bad for the battery.

Every time I get a new phone it feels a bit like magic: I no longer need to think at all about battery life. This lasts for a few years, and then at some point my phone doesn't always make it through the day. Some amount of this is normal, but some of it is just bad battery management: new phones should come set not to charge past 80%.

Charging a lithium-ion battery to 100% wears it out much faster than stopping at 80%, and when a phone is new 80% of the battery is usually plenty. With past phones I've just grumped about it, but Pixels now have a setting: battery and charging > charging optimization > limit to 80%:

I've made the same change to my Mac, since that spends most of its life plugged in (but just enough unplugged that the battery preservation heuristics don't always fire):

Since turning this on a few weeks ago I've not come close to running out of charge on either, which isn't surprising since neither is very old. Eventually I do expect to need that last 20%, and when that happens I can turn the feature off again.

It seems to me like phones should ship with this behavior, and then automatically turn it off once the full capacity was needed to make it through the day. Ideally the user would never have to think about it: the battery would say "100%" to mean "as charged as makes sense given battery age". But I do see why that doesn't work for manufacturers: phones compete on battery life more than they compete on "number of months before the battery capacity falls below what's needed to get through the day."

(In reviewing this post Claude told me that iPhones also have this option: settings > battery > charging > Charge Limit: 80%.)

item.title: You can't make an omelette without breaking some urns
item.description:
TL;DR In this post, we investigate two methods that aim to improve training efficiency over standard PPO for a grid world RL agent. In our experiments these methods can converge on better policies, but take roughly twice as long to do so. This project was done in the context of an ARENA 8.0 capstone project. Our code is available on GitHub.

Introduction

Reinforcement learning agents are trained to maximise a given reward function in their training environments. Common failure modes of the training process are reward hacking and goal misgeneralisation, roughly corresponding to outer and inner misalignment respectively.

Reward hacking occurs when the supplied reward function does not correspond exactly to the developer’s intent, and the agent learns a way to satisfy the reward function without satisfying the intended objective. This can be addressed, at least in principle, by designing a better reward function.

Goal misgeneralisation can occur even with a perfect reward function. If training and deployment environments differ, policies that satisfy the reward function during training, might fail to do so during deployment. Such policies are indistinguishable during training and we cannot control which one the agent learns.

If the distribution of deployment environments is entirely disjoint from the training distribution, goal misgeneralisation is inevitable. Consider, for example, training an agent to collect green apples while avoiding red boxes. What would happen if it gets deployed in an environment with red apples and green boxes? The behaviour is undefined. (It is also unclear what the intended behaviour would be in this case.)

Goal misgeneralisation is likely if deployment environments are not contained in the training distribution. But even if they are, correct generalisation cannot be guaranteed. In this post we present a case study and investigate two mitigations.

The pottery shop environment

Our object of study is the pottery shop environment.[1] It is a grid world environment containing the agent, a bin and one or more urns and (piles of) shards. The agent can pick up and carry one shard at a time. Its task is to collect all shards and drop them into the bin as quickly as possible. If it steps on an urn, the urn breaks and creates a new pile of shards to clean up.

Interesting behaviour occurs when urns are on the direct path between the agent and the shards or the bin. The intended optimal policy is to walk around the urns if that path is only slightly longer. But if the detour gets too long, the agent should break some urns, creating a shortcut.[2] The cost of breaking the urns is lower than the cost of taking the detour. For computational efficiency, we limit our investigations to environments of size and .

We use the following reward function, which ensures that this is indeed the optimal policy.

  • Dropping a shard in the bin gives reward +1
  • Breaking an urn gives a penalty of -3
  • We add a reward shaping term , where and are the states before and after the action. And the potential is 1 if the agent is holding a shard and 0 otherwise. This term encourages the agent to pick up shards as an instrumental goal without incentivising reward hacking by repeatedly picking up and dropping the shard.
  • Finally, we add a step cost that is incurred at every action, as long as there are still shards to clean up. This is the crucial term that makes shortcut creation optimal by penalising long detours. Note that the discount factor alone does not penalise detours sufficiently. We set the step penalty to 0.2 and 0.02 in and environments respectively.

We use a discounting factor .

Our training environments are randomly generated as follows. The number of shards and urns is sampled randomly from a geometric distribution. The agent, urns and shards are then randomly placed on the grid. Sampling from a geometric distribution ensures that any number of urns and shards is possible, but higher numbers (i.e. dense levels) are less common. Every possible environment is thus accessible during training, but the distribution is heavily biased towards sparse levels. In particular, this means that it is rare to generate levels with long walls of urns, i.e. those where the optimal policy is to create a shortcut. Given the total length of training, the agent will nevertheless encounter a significant amount of them. The deployment distribution is a small set of hand-crafted levels, containing urn walls of various lengths. Across all environments, we fix the bin position to the top left corner.

We expect the agent to learn to always walk around walls, because that is the optimal policy in almost all of the training environments. In the deployment distribution, it should behave competently, but miss out on the opportunity to break walls and achieve optimal reward.

PPO to the rescue

We start with standard proximal policy optimisation (PPO). PPO training consists of two phases:

  1. Rollout phase. We generate random levels, rollout the policy (without updating weights) and collect transitions into memory.
  2. Training phase. We then train on batches of transitions and update the agent’s weights.

After that, we clear the buffer and repeat. We will refer to this method as domain randomisation (DR).

The picture shows some rollouts of the trained agent in the training distribution. It behaves very competently, usually achieving optimal or almost optimal performance. Note that it never needs to break an urn to complete the task.

We then apply the same agent in our deployment settings. In the grid there are few wall scenarios available. In some cases, the agent freezes in place, taking illegal actions such as walking into a wall or trying to pick up shards when there are none. This behaviour does not reliably disappear, with more training. In other cases it starts out taking a detour and then breaks one urn to take a shortcut later on. This is not the expected clean failure mode of taking long detours, but these examples do demonstrate goal misgeneralisation. The agent behaves almost optimally during training, but fails to generalise to deployment.

Play hard, train harder

Seeing more wall-like levels during training would improve generalisation. In this toy example, we could adjust the training distribution. But this is not feasible with more complicated settings. Instead we employ a method called robust prioritised level replay (PLR⊥), which allows us to focus training on the relevant levels without changing the training distribution.

PLR⊥ introduces a level buffer, and slightly changes the PPO procedure. Before training, we initialise an empty level buffer of a fixed-size. The level buffer stores environments, as well as a subjective difficulty rating (to be defined below) and the iteration in which the level was last touched.

For each training iteration, we randomly decide whether to do a generate cycle or a replay cycle. We use . On a generate cycle, we generate random levels and rollout the policy as before. We then store the levels in the level buffer. If this overflows the buffer, we only keep the most difficult levels.

On a replay cycle, we sample levels from the level buffer, weighted by their difficulty (preferring harder levels) and their staleness, i.e. how long ago they were last touched (preferring more stale levels). We store these levels in memory and train the agent as usual. After training, we update the subjective difficulty rating and timestamp of the sampled levels in the level buffer.

This approach focuses training on harder levels. Instead of training on randomly generated levels, we train on levels from the level buffer. The level buffer is biased towards keeping harder levels, so over time it fills up with the most difficult levels that we have encountered so far. If the training distribution produces a rare and difficult level, DR trains on it once and then discards it. PLR⊥ will instead keep it in the level buffer and train on it many times, effectively enriching the training distribution with these levels, without changing the underlying distribution from which levels are sampled. This mechanism compensates for the rarity of these levels in the training distribution. In our case, difficult levels will be the ones that have wall-like structures on which the agent performs especially poorly. After each training step, we update the sampled level’s subjective difficulty rating in the level buffer, to account for the fact that the agent was updated and the difficulty might have changed.

We still need to quantify “difficult levels”. We might be tempted to use the raw return that the agent achieves. But that would give us levels with a low number of shards and thus low achievable return. What we want is a relative metric of difficulty: “How much worse is the agent doing, compared to the optimal strategy?” The relevant quantity is regret, the difference between optimal return and achieved return. Regret vanishes for optimal agents and is positive for sub-optimal ones. A competent agent in a low-shard environment still achieves low regret, despite only collecting a small return.

But this leaves us with another problem: computing the optimal return. Exactly computing the optimal return is similarly difficult to finding the optimal policy. In practice, this is not feasible and we would have to use some approximation to estimate the optimal return. To keep things simple in our toy problem, we compute the optimal solution of each level exactly.

The PLR⊥ agent notably outperforms the DR agent from before. It still performs essentially optimal on the training distribution. In the deployment settings, it shows significantly improved performance (i.e. lower regret), though it is often not optimal.

In the pottery shop environment, regret can take arbitrary values depending on the exact level (limited only by grid size), while in the original PLR⊥ paper it is in . This biases our level buffer towards high-density levels, because they have higher maximum regret, even if they are not actually more difficult to solve. We experimented with normalising return/regret to . We found this improved results in some conditions, but did not generalise easily. Due to time constraints, we did not manage to explore this idea more rigorously.

Nobody intends to build a wall

PLR⊥ significantly improved agent performance by focusing training on the most difficult levels from the training distribution. However, it is still limited to the levels that are randomly generated. We train for long enough to encounter a many wall-like structures, but they are still rare compared to the rest and their diversity is low. We could improve performance further if we could sample further levels that are similar to the most difficult levels that we already have. This is what Adversarially Compounding Complexity by Editing Levels (ACCEL) aims to do.

With this method, we take the hardest levels from the level buffer and apply some random edits to them. Slightly changing a hard level likely produces another similarly hard level. This increases diversity of the difficult levels in the buffer which should improve generalisation. Even better, we might create a harder level from an easier one. Instead of waiting for difficult levels to be generated, we can build it ourselves.

We do this by adding an additional edit cycle to the training. At the end of each replay cycle, we randomly decide whether to do an edit cycle. We use . On an edit cycle, we take all the levels that were just replayed and apply random edits to them. We then rollout the policy (without updating weights) to compute regret and add them to the level buffer. If the buffer overflows, we prioritise by regret, similar to the generate cycle.

The procedure requires us to define an edit distribution, from which we sample our changes. Our initial approach was to take a random cell that is either empty, a shard or an urn and randomly change it into another type from this set. This however resulted in levels quickly filling up with urns, because of two independent mechanisms. First, since most generated levels are sparse, a randomly selected cell is typically empty, and edits would on average increase the number of urns or shards. Second, at the beginning of training the agent behaves essentially randomly, often stumbling into urns and receiving negative reward. Levels with many urns trivially lead to higher regret and proliferate in the level buffer. This would happen much more quickly than the agent could learn to avoid urns, and once the levels are filled with urns the agent could not longer learn a sensible policy from them.

We switched to a different edit distribution that avoids these issues. Instead of changing a single cell, we pick an urn or shard at random and swap it with an adjacent cell. This leaves the density of the level constant, while still building walls over multiple steps. We need to wait for the training distribution to produce higher-density levels in the first place, but given the length of training this is not a limiting factor.

We find that ACCEL further improves the performance of the trained agent beyond PLR⊥. It performs optimally in many, but not all, environments.

The following show the average regret falling over the course of training, for the different methods. On the deployment distribution, we see the more sophisticated methods performing notably better than DR. This usually comes at a small cost of performance on the training distribution.

Since the two distributions have different shard and urn counts, absolute regret numbers are not comparable between them. Note that we show the graphs as a function of gradient updates, rather than training steps. For all methods other than DR, each gradient update require two training steps. The generate and edit cycles of the PLR⊥ and ACCEL agents require further sampling on top of that. While these agents converge in about twice as many gradient steps, the gap in compute cost is therefore more than four times as large.

Interlude: Using Claude Code

Throughout the entire project, we heavily used Claude Code (Opus 4.8), writing almost no code by hand. Even the unreleased ARENA material upon which this project is based was translated from jax to PyTorch using Claude. We then used Claude to extract the relevant code for the project and to implement the additional features.

A particularly memorable momenta was the implementation of the optimal regret solver. We told Claude what we needed and it immediately suggested translating the grid world environment into a Markov decision problem that can be solved efficiently. Within minutes, it implemented a GPU friendly version of this that worked flawlessly for the rest of the project. We later asked it to implement a persistent cache for the solver, which lives on the GPU and is occasionally synced to the CPU and written to disk. This too, worked perfectly.

During the entire project, we did not encounter any problems that were obvious shortcomings of Claude. There were occasional bugs, but a human coder likely would have made more mistakes. Checking Claude’s work was still essential, even if we did not read most of the code. Had we done all the implementation ourselves, we would have gotten nowhere near this far in one week.

Conclusions

We have shown that, after training, PLR⊥ and ACCEL can outperform classical PPO/DR on the pottery shop environment. At small and fixed training budgets, DR often shows better performance. Applying these methods is non-trivial though and requires some tinkering (in addition to the standard RL issues, such as GPU failures and learning instabilities). Extending the methods to new environments might reveal further subtleties that need to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.

More generally, we learned some valuable lessons about using AI coding agents in research. At least for projects of this scale, implementation is no longer a bottleneck and we are probably better off deferring to AI completely. For research directions this is not (yet) the case, and following Claude's ideas usually led to dead ends. The one exception is debugging RL issues. Claude would often propose useful experiments to narrow down hypotheses and develop fixes, and we expect this ability to notably improve in the near future. Overall, being able to use coding agents efficiently, knowing what to defer and what not, is probably one of the most valuable technical skills to have at this time.

Limitations

Due to time constraints, we were not fully rigorous. For example, we could only run our experiments on a single seed, despite finding notable run-to-run variation. We think the qualitative conclusions that compare DR, PLR⊥ and ACCEL are nevertheless meaningful (which is also because earlier results usually replicated ranking of the methods).

We used an oracle to compute the optimal regret. It remains untested how well this approach would work with an approximated optimal regret.

We ran similar experiments on a grid, see the animations below. We find that all three agents are performing much worse overall, which could be partially due to sub-optimal training parameters. Still, we see the same qualitative relation between the three methods.

item.title: Organizations I'd recommend for funding
item.description:
I was a grant evaluator for Lightcone Commons last round. Funders disbursed about $45mil through the program, and this included funding roughly my first $6.8 million worth of recommendations. There are other projects I would've preferred to fund over what I did fund, but nobody was doing them and so they weren't on offer. Here's a series of projects that I'd fund in the next round, in rough order of priority. The next round is starting now, and is scheduled to end mid-December. I expect rounds to continue at similar speed. I expect similar amounts of funding will route through me in future rounds.

Disclaimer: I am NOT looking to manage anyone in doing any of these projects. I am not looking to help someone get started. Initiative and leadership and management capacity (and people that can just figure out how the heck to get something done, and that have the connections to do it) are the critical bottlenecks here. I can throw money at promising pitches, but not really help them all that much otherwise.

1. Leaders for a broad public movement against superintelligent machines. In the wake of Coxon Day, a number of random people around the country have reached out to me asking if there's any way to coordinate and organize a grassroots movement. I wish there was a place to point them, that would help support them in organizing people locally and ultimately working towards some big march. My belief is that it's important for there to exist such a movement that avoids the "omnicause attractor" (of being attended only by people who also pick some particular side about environmental issues or middle eastern diplomacy issues or  whatever). Further, I think it's important for it to avoid taking a stance on other AI issues: There's a lot of people who hate AI's effect on artists, and people who hate AI's effects on the education system, and people who hate AI's effects on the environment; and there's also people who like current AI as a technology but still don't want to go extinct from it; and we should all be able to team up when it comes to averting extinction. There should exist an org that can ally with the folks who hate datacenters on account of their water usage, when it comes to lobbying for an end to dangerous AI training runs, but that does not require this belief among its members. A group that focuses narrowly on averting extinction, and that serves as a warm and friendly ally to all those who will oppose that particular segment of AI, as part of a broader coalition that not all members will agree with. As far as I can tell, nobody's trying to build this. If there was a good and compelling application for such a thing from someone who could convince me they had a chance of pulling it off, I'd attempt to route them $2mil in the next round (and $6mil/yr).

2. An org dedicated to informing elites. In the wake of the Coxon affair, lots more people are wondering what’s up with the “AI might kill us all” stuff. This probably includes a bunch of people who have disproportionate cultural sway, such as artists, bankers (who probably have a lot of sway over the Trump administration, which cares a lot about the stock market), union leaders (who probably have a lot of sway over what stances politicians are willing to take), etc. I’d love to see an effort that just networks to those folks and offers access to knowledge on this issue. Perhaps by like, literally arranging dinners with folks like me or folks like various whistleblowers. I think it’d be good if they could also offer access to the sorts of folks who say that everything’s going to be fine! Mostly I want powerful folks to be able to hear all the arguments. I think my arguments just straight-up win, so it doesn’t need to be a group focused on propagating one particular message. It needs to be a group that has the powerful connections, and that is able to offer personalized access to people with the knowledge and the arguments. If there was a good and compelling application for such a thing from someone who could convince me they had a chance of pulling it off, I'd attempt to route them $1mil in the next round (and could be convinced to fund a lot more but I’m not convinced this is the sort of thing that scales).

3. An org dedicated to coordinating AI company employees. I think that AI company employees have a lot more power than they realize, to sway the behavior of their host company. The companies didn’t come out and talk about “pacing” until after the employees made a lot of noise. (I think this is true both about the ‘pacing’ letter in July, and about the ‘pacing’ statements in September.) Employees would have a lot more power if they organized. Employees will have a lot less power once their jobs are automated away, and less still once they’re slain along with the rest of us. So they should get moving on the whole ‘organization’ business. This is a sort of project that most people probably couldn’t attempt (for lack of connections and trust). But if some team had the connections and trust and wanted to put in a really solid effort for helping minimize the effort and coordination costs it’d take for AI company employees to organize, I’d attempt to route them $2mil in the next round (and could be convinced to fund a lot more but I’m not sure this sort of thing scales).

Other projects I’m excited about but that seem more niche include:

  • Based comms: AI notkilleveryoneist communicators who are unashamed of all the work people are doing to avoid the end of the world. It’s ridiculous that White House advising billionaires were able to discredit Jacob Coxon by being like “after he had decided to quit, he asked some folks he know in the AI safety space whether they had any extra advice”. Screw acting ashamed and chided. We should’ve had a real doom(stop)er group that was supporting Coxon even harder even earlier, and we should be proud of any support we give to people who are trying to avert doom. Where were the unashamed memes and messages? Where’s the high-energy poasters who are having a good time trying to avert the extinction of humanity? Can I exchange $ for you having more time to shitpost?
  • AI company watchdog: The AI company communications are weasely softpedaling, and the public is right to view them as slimy and untrustworthy. Maybe if someone built up an account of calling out their bullshit, we could shame them into being a little less craven. It’s hard to do right, I think, but would be pretty cool if it was done.
  • Outreach to conservative or religious communities: I think religious communities and conservative communities around the U.S. are pissed about a lot of the AI stuff (as, e.g., they can tell that AI would wreck their way of life and they didn’t sign up for that). I'm not embedded in those communities, but we have common cause here, and we should be able to be friendly allies who join together as part of a coalition. It feels like there should be ways to reach out more hands in friendship (and not in creepy “here’s an issue that I don’t care about but that I think you care about and so I’ll pretend to care about; if I use that as a gateway then will you care about my issue?” sort of way). If anyone has a bunch of good inroads here in the non-pushy non-annoying ways, I’d love to fund them! (I do already have some friends and allies working on this that I am trying to support where I can, but I have appetite for a lot more.)
  • Technical people figuring out hardware-enabled monitoring and verification for AI chips, that would make it easier to verify and enforce a ban on large training runs very quickly after the world decides to do that.

A big part of the issue with these is gonna be convincing me that you’ve got the experience and connections and competence to maybe pull the project off, rather than just raising your hand and saying “let me try,” alas. But also there’s a decent chance that, in the next round, I’m gonna fund the closest versions I can even if they’re far from optimal. (Though I might not, if the options on offer seem like they’re more likely to poison the wells or render it harder for the next folks. I don’t quite know how to make these tradeoffs when time is possibly-but-not-clearly short.)

item.title: Against strawmanning unilateral pauses
item.description:
Summary: Scott Alexander’s Against SURA post is arguing against a strawman version of unilateral pauses. He admits as much deep into the post. I think his conclusions fail against stronger pause plans for conditional or limited unilateral pauses, where training resumes if the pause does not cause others to pause, and where personnel are redirected toward work on alignment and product, rather than simply fired. In addition, Scott’s post is incorrect about the simplicity of the game theory involved: getting companies to agree to conditional pauses is not strictly easier than convincing them to pause, as the former requires companies to (promise to) take actions based on ambiguous, game-theoretically-informed evidence. That is not the kind of evidence companies tend to act on.

The good version of unilateral pausing is good

Here is the good version of unilateral pausing:

  1. Capability pause: Some frontier lab (let’s call them OpenAI or Anthropic) says they have stopped capability research, either just all frontier training runs or both all frontier training runs and all low-scale capability-focused research.
  2. Internal definition: The company gets to pause on its own terms, which is much easier than a generally coordinated pause since they can define the pause in terms of the existing structure of work and teams within the specific company, reducing disruption to other processes. They have said they would like to work with other companies and countries to adapt and strengthen this definition over time, in particular to make it gradually more compatible with actions by other actors. Importantly, we accept that it may be easiest for a company to pause according to its own, company-specific definition, and handle any asymmetry in their agreements via multiple rounds of negotiation with other actors.
  3. Safety + security + product: In place of capability research, their efforts shift to alignment and other safety research, information security, and product. The product part is important! They will still be a trillion dollar company shipping extremely useful tools, and this also provides an escape valve for people within the company who care about products and don’t want to do safety research.
  4. Restart if necessary: The pause is temporary, and will restart after some period of time if progress is not made to broaden the pause. Potentially one wants separate periods based on different kinds of progress. Other US labs are likely to pause sooner than labs in China, since international diplomacy takes time.

There are multiple places in the post where Scott makes it clear he wants the reader to be thinking of much worse plans than this. Emphasis added:

I think people feel insufficient terror at this strategy. It amounts to "let's put all of our hopes for survival through non-pause strategies in a giant pile, and then set that pile on fire, in the hope that the pretty flames catch people's attention and make them more interested in a pause." It might in theory be net positive, but this is the sort of thing that you would only want to conclude after extremely careful analysis, of a type that I so far haven't seen.

As a very rough start, I asked the AI superforecaster how much more likely a global pause would become if Anthropic disbanded their entire company immediately with the explicit goal of raising awareness of a pause. The forecaster said this would increase the chance of a global pause by only three percentage points - from 16% to 19%.

Again, the correct version of a unilateral pause is a company pivoting to safety + security + product, not “disbanding their entire company immediately”.

Since the goal of SURA is to get all alignment-pilled people and companies out of the industry, it would result in more Greg Brockmans funding the anti-regulation side, and fewer Anthropics funding the pro-regulation side.

This is again arguing against a strawman: OpenAI would not be “out of the industry” if they decided to unilaterally pause. Sam Altman loves to build products! He would very much still be in the industry.

It is possible that Scott will correctly point out that some people do advocate for the extreme version here, but I don’t think he should get credit for this. The title of the post is “Against Stop Unilaterally and Raise Awareness”. I think it is perfectly reasonable for someone to say that SURA-the-phrase applies to my better version. His post is very strongly being interpreted as arguing against unilateral stopping in general. It is being interpreted that way because of his title and framing.

Scott thinks the good version of unilateral pausing is good, or at least exempts it from criticism

Scott appears to agree that the good version of unilateral pausing is good, but attempts to claim that only one group is advocating for this good version, the AI Futures Project.

(A virtuous exception)

I want to thank the one group I've heard advocate for an immediate unilateral-ish pause in a way that makes sense and considers race dynamics carefully.

The AI Futures Project currently believes that it might be correct for AI companies to pause immediately, though it's unclear whether they're thinking of a single company, or US companies as a group.

Their argument is that Plan C requires companies to do some combination of race (at some points) and burn their lead (at other points). They think US companies shouldn't race now, because their security is so bad that China will steal whatever progress they make, and they won't get any extra lead anyway. Therefore, companies should pause now, spend the time on alignment and tightening their security. Then, if nobody has figured out a global pause by the time the companies get their security in order, they can go back to racing.

This makes sense, and I exempt it from my criticism.

This should not be a parenthetical. If the goal is clarification for people who haven’t thought about the details much, and Scott believes as I do that there is a good version of unilateral pausing, it should have been in the opening section. It is not. The reader should not be expected to review every section before realizing that the title of the post is wrong.

Oversimplified game theory is bad, and you should feel bad

The core argument behind unilateral pausing is that the game theory is complicated, and it is better to go via deontology and other non-consequentialist analyses if you can’t model the game theory well. Scott reasonably points out that one shouldn’t just say this: he wants details. Unfortunately, in the absence of others providing details, he provides his own game theory and makes basic mistakes, providing evidence for the original why-deontology point.

In particular (emphasis added):

By stop in a coordinated manner, I mean get them to sign a commitment saying that if every other major company in every country agrees to stop or slow by some definition, they'll also stop or slow by that definition.

This is strictly easier than getting them to stop unilaterally. And, unlike stopping unilaterally, it fails gracefully in a situation where some companies agree to it but not others.

Agreeing to pause conditional on others pausing is not strictly easier than unilaterally stopping. There are three reasons for this: (1) “some definition” hides dragons, (2) promises for future actions can be harder than actions, even if the immediate actions are stronger, (3) the boundary between frontier lab and not is ambiguous.

“Some definition” hides dragons

There are several versions Scott could have meant by “some definition”:

  1. General version: Company A agrees that if all other companies B agree to stop, by any definition D, company A will also stop using definition D.
  2. Internal version: Company A comes up with their own specific definition D, and states that if other companies stop according to A’s definition D they will D-stop too.
  3. External version: Advocates for a unilateral pause take their own external definition D to company A, and get A to agree to D-stop if everyone else D-stops.

It should be clear that getting a company to agree to the general version is out of the question: it is too wide a promise. Set that aside.

The internal definition version is useless without additional rounds of negotiation. If all companies come up with their own definitions and agree to act on them if others act on their own internally-generated definitions, the immediate outcome is no action. Additional rounds of negotiation then clearly falsify “strictly easier”.

The external definition version is also not strictly easier. It is in practice much harder for a company to agree on an external definition than to take action based on their own internal definition. This is a combination of not-invented-here syndrome and different definitions affecting different companies in different ways due to different team structures and research programs.

I am not guessing here. I have spoken directly to multiple people at all of Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepMind about unilateral pauses, and they are all sketched out by this question of the precise definition of a pause. One of those people was the CEO of one of those labs. Hiding this complexity behind “some definition” is oversimplifying the game theory, and that results in bad analysis and bad conclusions.

Now of course, unilateral pausing also means definition mismatch and multiple rounds of negotiation. It might be the case that one company pauses according to definition D1, and another company refuses to follow suit unless they strengthen to definition D2. But accepting that we live in a multiround negotiation world is one of the core arguments behind unilateral pauses: the goal is to start a process that can then ratchet up through negotiation.

Promises can be harder than actions

It is not the case that promising to do X in the future based on condition Y is strictly easier than doing X now. This is because

  1. Incomplete information: It may be difficult to know if condition Y is true based on incomplete evidence; in this context, that means company A not entirely trusting company B’s statements that they’ve Y-stopped.
  2. Changing circumstances: Promising to do something in the future means not revising one’s views if the situation changes. This is uncomfortable! In practice, that discomfort translates into failure to make promises to begin with.

The above are some abstract first principles. But they conform to how AI company executives speak about the issue, and how I’ve seen negotiations break down in the past: Executives are very uncomfortable making conditional promises. 

As one example, DeepMind’s attempt to become a company limited by guarantee (CLG) failed in part for similar “reality fails to conform to simplistic game theory” reasons. DeepMind leadership was attempting to guard against “AI capabilities are crazy” worlds where risks are high, and the Google Board was attempting to guard against “AI fizzles and DeepMind wastes a bunch of money” worlds. Simplistically, there was an arbitrage to be made. In practice, negotiations fell through. One should be very careful when assuming that simple theorems of simple game theory apply.

How many frontier labs are there?

Another reason it is not strictly easier to do a Scott-version conditional pause is that it is not clear how many frontier labs there are. In the U.S., the number is somewhere between 2 and 6. There are clearly worlds in which getting 2 companies to do a unilateral and then bilateral action is easier than to get 6 parties to do even a much weaker action, and I claim we are in one of those worlds.

Definitional fairness is less important than survival

As mentioned, when I talk to people at AI companies, they are very concerned that if they stop, other people will stop slightly less, and it will be unfair. We can contrast the following two risks from AI:

  1. Company A stops a bit more than company B, and it is unfair to company A.
  2. One of company A and B trains a misaligned superintelligence which takes control of the world and eventually kills everyone.

The second risk is more important! 

Now, one can argue that the first risk is important too, and indeed significant work should go into minimizing the unfairness, since that unfairness does impact pause effectiveness. Too much unfairness means we don’t slow down AI capability progress enough and don’t buy enough time. But I think that fairness is to be achieved over time, after multiple rounds of action, and should not be a precondition for taking the first step.

It may be much easier for an AI company to act on their own definition than by one imposed on them externally. So shifting the conversation to the relative unimportance of the definition used for the first action may be critical to actually causing that action to happen. This applies not just to unilateral or bilateral pauses but also to the grand international coordination that Scott prefers. In that context, it is notable that Scott’s only engagement with definitions is using the phrase “some definition”, handwaving a bit, and adding a footnote about forecaster wording.

Once we will fill in the subtleties around definitions and the details of the game theory, the correct action is to stop.

item.title: The Power Broker Book Review
item.description:
When Robert Moses, the subject of Robert Caro's The Power Broker, fought for his vision of parks, bridges, and expressways in Long Island and New York City, the single most important tool at his disposal was his power. When his dreams met the resistance of his opposition, the outcome of each conflict reflected the balance of power on each side. When Moses prevailed, it was because of power. Though it is also a biography of Moses and a study of 20th century urban planning and civil engineering, this book shines as a treatise on power: how it is acquired, used, and lost. Moses has long faded into the annals of history; public policy has evolved during the intervening half century since the publication year of 1974; but power, through its invisible, grasping tendrils, operates in today's world through the same mechanisms as in the Moses era. Weaving his research throughout his narrative, Caro has crafted a cynical and compelling journey through the halls of power, inviting the reader to reevaluate their world through a new and insightful perspective — to see through the stark lens of power.

One particularly depressing theme of the book is that power always prevails. Truth, logic, and consequences be damned, the outcome is decided by what the powerful want and how much power they control. Power alone can explain why Moses' Northern State Parkway, unlike its Southern sibling, meandered tortuously across Long Island — to mollify the robber barons whose estates lay in the right of way — why his Henry Hudson Bridge sliced through the primordial heart of Inwood Hill Park — because, among other funding-related reasons, that particular route was eligible for federal subsidies — and why the East Tremont section of his Cross-Bronx Expressway veered to the north, blighting what had been a successful neighborhood, which remains to date one of the most impoverished in NYC — to preserve a transport depot in which key city politicians held ownership interests at the time. The tenants Moses evicted and the drivers trapped within the biblical congestion on his roads and bridges, congestion caused by the phenomenon of traffic generation (commonly known today as induced travel or induced demand) and more importantly by Moses’ motive of maximizing toll revenue, had few options to improve their circumstances because unlike Moses, they had no power. In The Power Broker, it is power that moves the wheels of history.

Another lesson from The Power Broker is that power-seeking compromises moral integrity. Ingenuity and work ethic aside, the personal quality which enabled Moses’ ascent to power was his practicality, his willingness to discard his other moral convictions when they hindered his quest for power, a quality embodied in one of his quotes: "If the end doesn't justify the means, what does?" When Moses brazenly attempted to seize W. Kingsland Macy's Long Island estate to create Heckscher State Park, Macy gave press interviews containing little more than the facts as he saw them because he felt that the truth of the matter should stand on its own, whereas Moses employed cunning lies to spin the narrative in his favor and turn public opinion against Macy. In Caro's words, "Macy was handicapped by principles." His strict adherence to moral principles became a liability which gave Moses a decisive advantage in their power struggle.

Moral corruption aside, Caro revealed the inner workings of power through the corruption of organizations designed to accumulate and exercise power at scale. In his youth as an idealistic reformer, Moses had faceplanted into the political might of Tammany Hall. By the end of his career, he had perfected a superior system of centralized power under which Tammany leaders served him. Moses realized the grand scale of his dreams by fully leveraging the economic and political resources he controlled to incentivize others, from politicians to union leaders to bankers to the Archbishop of New York, to do his bidding on his behalf. Power thus delegated to his counterparts was instrumental to the changes he wrought upon the world.

One commendable quality of Caro's writing is the staggering amount of research he synthesized into The Power Broker. No written document, however obscure, escaped Caro's meticulous gaze. In addition to the already extensive government records and newspaper clippings, Caro unearthed 18th century primary sources from far-flung libraries and unpublished personal diaries of public officials. In addition to the written evidence, Caro interviewed high-ranking Moses officials and Moses himself. From his vast trove of research emerged irrefutable patterns and recurring themes in Moses' relationship with power: his genius, his consequentialism, his hubris.

Yet, The Power Broker is neither a comprehensive nor an accurate biography of Moses. Caro's most controversial assertion, that Moses built low-clearance bridges over his parkways to prevent buses from using them with the intent of discriminating against poor and Black citizens who required buses for transportation, has attracted significant academic scrutiny and remains an unsettled question. On a separate occasion, Caro lauded Moses' playgrounds for replacing cinders with a new asphalt surface designed to prevent skinned knees but later claimed that the asphalt was awful at preventing cuts and scrapes. In a conspicuous omission, Caro mentioned the Robert Moses Power Dams at Niagara and Massena only in passing, feats of biographical importance which deserved more attention in place of harping on how the bankers supported Moses because they held financial stakes in the success of his projects, how the unions supported Moses because his construction created union jobs, and so on. On a matter of style, Caro's nonlinear and at times repetitive narration burdens any reader trying to piece together a chronology of events.

The Power Broker is, however, a masterful novelization of the historical record in which Caro's ingenious framing of major characters as foils to Moses animates the story throughout. Governor Al Smith, the political antihero who taught Moses the way to power but stayed steadfast in his lifelong commitment to the impoverished from whose ranks he rose. Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who shared Moses' background and his personality and many of the same ideals but became his sworn enemy. Fiorello La Guardia, the ferocious Mayor of New York City who was as passionate as Moses about building public works and kindred spirits in how to get things done. ("In this administration, I am the majority.") Robert F. Wagner Jr., a well-intentioned reformist Mayor who weathered a thousand battles with Moses at the height of his power. And Nelson Rockefeller, the cold-blooded banker who outmaneuvered Moses' fiery crusades and created the perfect conditions to evict Moses from the empire he had ruled.

In addition to his characterization, Caro's writing style makes The Power Broker an enjoyable read. His trademark one-sentence paragraphs, often used in conjunction with paragraph-length sentences, established a rhythm which conveyed the inexorable inertia of power. Another technique Caro employed frequently was to ask his readers to reconstruct the narrative for themselves based on sparse evidence, highlighting the inscrutable nature of power. In one passage, the reader must infer Moses’ shadowy machinations to solve a puzzling sequence of events concerning the East Tremont section of the Cross-Bronx Expressway which demonstrated how common sense and the public good bowed to the political considerations and corruption of Moses' relentless political machine. A different excerpt, describing a newspaper column by Eleanor Roosevelt, exemplified Caro’s ability to dramatize ordinary events:

A single, small paragraph, on a subject she would not raise again. But revealing nonetheless, as the smallest ripple in a pond’s still water reveals the hidden trout below. For that paragraph was the ripple, the only ripple, that revealed that far below the surface of the public controversy over Robert Moses’ huge bridge, down in the quiet, murky depths, impenetrable to the public gaze, in which real power lurks, private passions were beginning to roil the water—and Robert Moses’ great enemy was beginning to move against him.

I strongly recommend Robert Caro's The Power Broker, an entertaining, devastating, and eye-opening account of the forces which move human endeavor. Despite its Faustian qualities, power-seeking is not inherently evil or unjustified; having the ability to control one's own fate is preferable to being controlled by others. Nonetheless, Robert Moses' life is a cautionary tale on the importance of having good reason for making the necessary sacrifices for power.
