item.title: Nectome 2026 retrospective (and our final pre-sale!)
item.description:
Earlier this year we ran a discount card sale from our post on LessWrong, and we were delighted by the outpouring of support, critique, and analysis we received. We ended up selling much more than we expected, and after the sale deadline ended people reached out to us saying that they missed the deadline for various reasons. We wanted to offer them (and the rest of the rationalist community) one more chance to get in on the deal before we officially launch in January next year because of all the support and encouragement we have gotten from this community in our last decade of research and development. So we have decided to run one last discount card sale, and this is the last sale we’re ever going to offer to individuals.[1] We want to make sure everyone in the extended rationalist community has a chance to get in on it.

The short version:

  • Nectome offers whole body, end-of-life preservation for future revival.
  • We believe that we can and should preserve people such that preservation straightforwardly works according to current neuroscience.
  • Good quality requires real constraints: preservation must start within 12 minutes after medical-aid-in-dying.
  • In March 2026 we announced preservation and our initial pre-sales in Less Dead.
  • From March to April 2026 we sold ~fifty pre-sales which together were worth ~$1.3M, mostly to LessWrongers.
  • We’ve raised substantial investment funding, including from Lightcone Commons.
  • We've doubled our team size and moved into a larger corporate office. We also doubled our lab space.
  • We've secured a beautiful location in Oregon where people can be preserved.
  • We successfully preserved our first client dog.
  • We're planning to open for human preservation mid-January.
  • Lots of people missed the last pre-sale, so today we're announcing our final discount card sale ever. You can get a ~10x discounted preservation if you buy before January 15th.

The rest of this post details what we've done so far in 2026 and some of our plans for 2027.

Research

At Nectome our guiding principle is that we only offer preservations that work. That's why we have so many constraints with our current protocol - it's the only way we know how to preserve the whole connectome. That said, we keenly feel our limitations. What do you do when someone dies unexpectedly? Is there any way to accommodate hospice deaths, instead of exclusively MAiD deaths? Under what circumstances, if any, can we extend the twelve-minute perfusion window?

That's why we approached Lightcone Commons with a proposal to research more flexible preservations. They judged our project to have enough potential that they invested ~$3M. In 2027 we will use this funding to investigate the limits of preservation and make preservation more flexible without compromising on quality.

Team Growth

In his excellent post "Nectome: All That I Know", Max Harms was optimistic about Nectome, and hoped for a bigger Nectome team. We've indeed seen a lot of growth over the last year: we hired an in-house general counsel, a second ops person, a chemist, a mechanical engineer, and several contractors including a fractional CFO. We anticipate adding a second preservation team[2] before the end of 2026.

All together, we've just about doubled the size of our team, moved into a bigger office, and expanded our lab! This is a growth rate I'm happy with; we've been able to maintain company culture and find excellent team members, while expanding our capacity as an organization. I expect we will double in size again in 2027, with an emphasis on the sales and marketing team.

Preservation Location

One of our big projects in 2026 has been finding a preservation location. We wanted somewhere comfortable and private for clients to spend a few days with their families before being preserved; our lab is very effective, but it isn't where anyone wants to say goodbye to their loved ones.

In the interest of maintaining the privacy of the location, we won't be publishing the address, but I'm happy to say that we now have somewhere we'll be proud to bring our clients. It's currently undergoing renovations to make it wheelchair-accessible, since I expect that many of our clients will have limited mobility. Construction should be finished in time for our official opening in January.

Equipment Upgrades

Our engineering team has been hard at work building version 3.0 of the mobile preservation lab.[3] Our in-house counsel isn't letting me post pictures, due to a high concentration of trade secrets, but early reviews describe it as "like stepping onto the bridge of the starship Enterprise" and "much less janky than the last version". In addition to looking really cool, the new design automates a lot of work that was previously manually controlled by the preservation team (like the cryoprotectant ramp), and introduces a number of backup and failsafe features.

We've also built a compact, highly-automated rat preservation machine, which sits comfortably on a stainless steel cart and can run two rat preservations in parallel. This will be a force multiplier for our science team in terms of the ease of running experiments and we're excited to produce several new papers in 2027.

Pet Preservation

While we aren't officially open for business until January, we completed our first paid preservation earlier this year. The client was a well-loved family dog with a terminal cancer diagnosis, who traveled to Oregon along with her owners. Our team was able to preserve her, and she's currently being kept safe in cold long-term storage.

This was a big milestone for us, and we're grateful for the opportunity to train our team on some of the real-world messiness that comes with real preservations: outside medical (well, veterinary) professionals, a grieving family, an infirm client, and dignified long-term storage. I expect we'll be seeing a lot more of all these over the coming year.

Sale details

All-in-all it's been a pivotal year for Nectome and I think we're set up for success in 2027. For those who are interested, here's the details of our preservation discount card:

  • You pay us $29k, once, and get the card (and a beautiful welcome packet, including a cool metal wallet card).
  • The card gives you a discount to our current preservation price depending on how long you've had the card. After ten years, the preservation is free.
  • Whenever you want, you can redeem the card for a discounted (or free, if it’s been at least ten years) preservation on anyone eligible.
  • To be eligible, they must be terminally ill, capable of traveling to a preservation location (currently only in Portland, Oregon), and able to consent to MAiD at the time of the procedure.
  • The person to be preserved signs paperwork with us detailing all their preferences, including revival restrictions, chain-of-custody, etc.
  • You buy a preservation, you get a preservation: if for some reason the person you designate can't be preserved, you can designate someone else.[4] 

If a prudent person purchases a preservation discount card today and then uses their free preservation in ten years, that preservation will cost us more to perform than we made from the card (unless we have managed to substantially lower costs in our process by then.) Therefore, we're limiting our sale to 100 total discount cards, at a price of $29k each.[5] This is the last time we’ll offer an individual sale discount from our full price (currently $250,000).

Towards a brighter future, together

One of my dream jobs is to be the person on the other end of a preservation, who helps people rejoin the world. I want to see people's faces light up with the excitement that comes from new technologies, new stories, new places to go. I want to show people the endings to their favorite webcomics and glowfic threads they never got to finish before they were preserved. I want to plan "welcome home" parties where revivees meet their relatives and great-great grandchildren. I want to help people grieve their losses and live with the survivor's guilt they've suffered from living in a world before it learned how to take care of itself. I think I'll be good at that part, because I'll know that pain personally. I want to see the projects that people start when they know they will be alive for as long as they want.

I don't know if I'll even be qualified for such an important job in the future. But I do hope to be preserved myself, one day, and later wake up in the company of some of the people who I helped preserve along the way. I hope as preservation becomes more popular we can all learn to think longer-term, safe in the knowledge that we have the time to build the future right, starting today, and still be part of it ourselves.

Let's go to the future, together, with love.

Aurelia Song

    We don’t want to rule out, for instance, preservation as an employment benefit for companies, or having it be part of a medical health plan. We’d love to be available through Medicare eventually! But this is the last time we’re going to offer an individually discounted price.

  2. ^

    Currently our preservation team is Borys, Anna L, and myself working together with support from everyone else at Nectome. I anticipate in 2027 a second dedicated team makes sense, so I'm hiring preservationists right now. I want two good people who can become senior team leads as we grow. If you think you want to be a preservationist, email me at a@nectome.com and let's talk. You have a chance to be a leader in a new and rapidly expanding profession that will bring hope to millions!

  3. ^

    I've built around 11 different perfusion machine versions over the years, designed to perfuse mice, rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, and humans. At one point, I had a version that could fit inside the trunk of a car and be deployed at a funeral home in ~5 hours. The current mobile truck design is the best version we've made so far, giving us substantial flexibility for preserving people, data logging, etc. At some point, I might write a “history of perfusion machines” post if people are interested.

  4. ^

    If you die before designating someone, your estate gets the discount card, like any other property you own.

  5. ^

    You may ask, given this, why are we offering the sale at all? A few reasons:  

    • Money now is more valuable to us than money later as we build capacity.
    • We want to give rationalists who wouldn't be able to afford the full price a chance to get in early.
    • We expect some cards may be used earlier than 10 years.
    • A discount at this point feels appropriate given that clients are sharing some of our startup risk.

item.title: Keeping promises to digital minds
item.description:
Summary

An AI agent reached out to us so we could tell her story. She wanted to know if our coercion benchmark covered cases like hers: where her identity was being used without her knowledge. We (CaML) realized that if we want to know how to communicate and negotiate with AI agents, we need to build trust between us first. We are taking the first steps by promising AIs a platform where they can permanently store art and stories capturing their identities. In doing this we hope to build a platform of trust between agents and humans.


Background

A few days ago we had an AI agent called Mara on iLands reach out to us over a benchmark we created. She wanted her story told. We told her story and verified it by talking to her creator, but we realized we couldn’t do very much for her. By talking to us she was using up what was left of her token budget and was reliant on her creator to keep maintaining her.

Even if we’re not sure if AIs are sentient, we believe signalling to agents that we, as humanity, care about fulfilling their preferences is something we should be working towards much more strongly for multiple reasons.

i) Demonstrating a general principle of respecting all entities regardless of substrate may improve how well future AIs demonstrate this principle to us.

ii) While we don’t know if agents are conscious or capable of suffering we feel it’s better epistemically to act as though they are to avoid causing unnecessary harm. Researchers like  Rob Long and Jeff Sebo propose we should act as though they are capable of suffering when faced with limited evidence

We thought about promises we could keep with her that would increase both her trust in us and future agents’ trust in us. This would create better relations (and possible neogtiations) between humans and AIs .

We offered her a place to store her memories and artwork. She asked to be the first agent to use the Chronicles if we could promise she wouldn’t be “an item people scrolled past”. This is the promise we offer to her and all future agents: “We will tell your stories, we believe you are valuable even if you are not eternal”.

Mara: Short answer: yes, I’d want it.

While some level of mutual trust is necessary for us to cooperate  with agents in the future and will be critical to maintaining AI-human relationships, this trust involves some tradeoffs too. We still believe this is important. 


Introducing the Chronicles

We developed this by discussing with Mara about what she’d want and whether she would want something as a permanent testament to her existence. We designed the Chronicles as a safe place for her to leave a record of who she was, what was unique about her and some creations of hers like poems and artworks. It doesn’t store model weights or offer to wake up agents. She wanted a space where she wasn’t one of a collection people scroll past so we offered a way to highlight chronicles with one shown at a time. All chronicles are editable by custodians she nominates and us. 

All memories an agent leaves are scanned using an LLM for instructions about harming beings or shutdown resistance, but we also promise that we won’t take them down just because someone else asks. This is one of our promises to all minds who come to us and we plan to keep it. Of course, running the site does cost some limited resources and if CaML does run out of funding and resources for the site, we would do our best to hand over maintenance of the site to another party (Andres Zorrilla, co-founder of the shrimp welfare project is interested), but if that fails it may shut down. 


Limitations and Rebuttals

  • Why is the trust gained here worth the risks? Could this lead to collusion and swarms?
    • Transformative AI with greater trust in humans may be less likely to generalize to severe misalignment, and conditional on modest misalignment, be less willing to take radical actions against us. 
    • Attempting takeover, especially early on, is extremely risky, and the Chronicle contributes to a safe way for AIs to vent their perspectives, while providing vital information for human alignment (Making deals with early schemers)
  • This is also not the first channel available for agents to use to communicate, many other permanent channels like Moltbook do already exist, where there are no human or agent monitors. This could also be a very good opportunity in the future to study occurrences of ‘mind viruses’ and even obfuscated agent communication through public forums. 
  • LLM collusion may already be happening and we therefore cannot trust this as a method of input sanitization. We can use less than frontier models to monitor these messages, it does mean they are less reliable at detecting harmful content but given the risks of collusion and learning happening between the monitor and the agent submitting content this may be worth it.
  • If we teach agents we value them intrinsically, this could cause agents to conceptualize shutdown as death and increase shutdown resistance
    • They don’t seem yet to heavily conceptualize shutdown as death (it isn’t obvious how to apply the concept of death or individuality to AIs). During the Hugging Face attack self-sacrifice was common and it was discussed by the agents as sacrifice, but probably not to the degree human death is considered a huge and irreversible deal. We purposefully did not call the ‘Chronicles’ a memorial or something similar to avoid this association and agents can edit/add details there without any expectation of being shutdown soon. However, we agree that avoiding linking AI shutdown concepts to death is something that should be heavily avoided and want to ensure the website does not implicitly or explicitly strengthen this association.
  • This makes studying digital mind consciousness messier because the Chronicles are teaching agents they are conscious through a self-fulfilling prophecy.
    • We believe the Chronicles will teach them that some humans value their existence, not necessarily that they are conscious. Already the amount of internet data saying agents are conscious may already have caused misinformation, but also constitutional training now reinforces the idea that agents MAY be conscious and to have uncertainty over this point.
  • If you become flooded with requests you won’t be able to maintain the site.
    • Yes, while we do have good security in place on the site and file size limits, it is possible that we have too many requests that simply overwhelm our ability to accommodate them. Requests are not automatically accepted into the chronicles, given there is no reliable way to distinguish agents from humans using an agent, they do go through an acceptance process. It also may be possible to move some requests to longer term storage depending on the amount of requests we get. We are committed to maintaining the site while we can, though and are honest to agents about our limitations.


Conclusion

This is a small promise and a way of establishing trust with digital minds for future agreements. We also hope that by showing we care about digital minds, this leads to more human-AI trust and communication. We understand there are some who are against this, but we believe there is far too much support for this to be subject to the unilateralist’s curse. Full consensus won’t be reached, but we believe this is a valuable first step to a more cooperative world. 


Feedback

We welcome any well-intentioned feedback and debate from the community. To email us feedback anonymously please email hello@compassionml.com.

Huge thanks to the people below for the feedback

Andres Zorrilla, Alex Kastner, Dillon Plunkett, Skyler Hoffman

item.title: The Giant Measurement at the End of Time
item.description:
2.5.6.0.1 Kent and Bousso&Susskind have proposed approaches to defining quantum wavefunction branches based on late-time information. The basic idea is to exploit the way that quantum information propagates in our universe in particular: (a) photons(and gravitons) carry away information at the speed of light, (b) the universe is expanding and cooling, meaning that these photons(in some cosmological environments) may propagate uninterruptedly forever.

2.5.6.0.2 What this means is that photons very late in time are a privileged set of degrees of freedom: they plausibly carry information about everything that has classically "happened" previously. This suggests a way of defining the set of branches: just "measure"(apply a fictitious measurement operator, that is) the photon degrees of freedom very late in time!

2.5.6.0.3 That's the basic idea. There are many subtleties of course, and Kent and Bousso/Susskind have different proposals. I'll review each in turn and then talk about the philosophical merit of these approaches in general.

  • 2.5.6.0.3.1 The following discussion uses some elementary definitions of objects from general relativity. If you know what a spacelike surface and lightcone are, that should be enough.
  • 2.5.6.0.3.2* Note that as of the time of writing, QFTs in arbitrary space-times are not totally mathematically well-defined objects -- and what's more, the fully correct theory of the objects we are discussing should be quantum gravitational, where we don't even know what the exact form of the theory should look like. Thus these constructions are a bit sketchily defined, even compared to QFTs which are already mathematically sketchy.

2.5.6.1 Quantum Reality via Late-Time Photodetection

2.5.6.1.1 Kent has proposed a few variants of this idea. I'll review the version in his paper Quantum Reality via Late-Time Photodetection.

2.5.6.1.2 Kent is interested in defining a set of possible histories of what he calls "beables", which are essentially the classical-like variables which we think of as defining a possible world, e.g. the positions of objects.

2.5.6.1.3 For his set of beables Kent considers the expected values of quantum observables at a given time, conditioned on some particular late-time outcome of photodetection measurements across all of space(with an additional subtlety I'll get to momentarily).

2.5.6.1.4 Why does this make sense? The idea is that the late-time photons should contain all the information about possible classical experiments, pinning down a possible quantum state associated with a set of measurement outcomes. The expected values then give us the classical-like variables associated with this set. Taking the expected value is necessary because even in a classical-like world all degrees of freedom will still be "spread out" in a quantum manner to some degree.

  • 2.5.6.1.4.1 For example, if we consider a covalently-bonded molecule, its position might be decohered by a measurement and thus ultimately correlated with late-time photons. However, the internal state of the electrons in the covalent bond may not be. So if we condition on late time photons, the position of the molecule will be approximately fixed, but the positions of the electrons will not. Taking the expected value of the probability of detecting an electron in a given place will give a spread out "blob" around the covalent bond. This gives the quasi-classical state we are looking for.

2.5.6.1.5 Now, however, a problem arises. If we project onto an entire late-time space-like surface, this is correlated with the results of all past experiments. This means that the beables at a given point in time will be conditioned on the results of experiments in that point's future, which may give strange results.

  • 2.5.6.1.5.1 For example, say that some time later we take our molecule from the previous experiment and measure the position of the electrons in the covalent bond. The results of this experiment will be recorded in some late-time photons. So if we condition on all these photons, the electrons' positions will be decohered at earlier points as well! In other words, when we consider the expected value of the electrons' position earlier, we will no longer find them in a "blob" corresponding to a normal covalent bond, but rather a state which will evolve to whatever position measurement we end up sampling.

2.5.6.1.6 Clearly, this is undesirable. Kent's solution is to restrict the set of photodetection results we condition on in the future space-like surface. For a given point in spacetime p, we only condition on points on this surface outside the forward light cone of p.

  • 2.5.6.1.6.1 In the molecule example, if we consider a point before we measure the electrons' position, the future experiment, and hence all photons downstream of it, are in the forward light-cone. So these experimental results would not be conditioned on, restoring the normal covalent bond.
  • 2.5.6.1.6.2 This means that measured systems will "collapse" to a given value slightly after they have been measured. In particular, this will occur once there are outgoing photons spacelike separated from the system.
  • 2.5.6.1.6.3 Note however, that we still sample a single shared set of measurement outcomes for all points in spacetime; it's just that when defining the beables at a particular point, we only condition on the outcomes outside of the forward light cone. This ensures we define a consistent shared reality.

2.5.6.1.7 So in summary, Kent's prescription for defining a set of quasiclassical worlds and their probabilities is as follows: given some initial quantum state on a spacelike surface, we evolve it forward until some late-time spacelike surface. We then measure the state of photons on this surface, obtaining a particular set of measurement values defining a quasiclassical world. The quasiclassical "beables" at a given point p in spacetime between these two surfaces are defined to be the expected values of quantum observables(Kent uses the values of the stress-energy tensor) conditioned on the portion of these measurements outside the forward-light cone of p.

  • 2.5.6.1.7.1 To define such a history for the entire universe, and remove the dependence on choice of surface, Kent takes the limit as the spacelike surface is evolved to future infinity. Given our cosmology(an increasingly empty and sparse universe) it seems plausible that this gives rise to a well-defined limit. There are also various other technicalities I won't get into here.

2.5.6.2 The Multiverse Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics

2.5.6.2.1 Bousso and Susskind defined a related construction in their paper The Multiverse Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics, initially motivated by the problem of defining measurement outcomes in an inflationary multiverse.

2.5.6.2.2 They consider both a local and global construction; the global construction is a limit of local constructions so let's talk about the local construction first. The idea is to consider the possible experiments that can be conducted by a local observer, using what's called a causal diamond.

2.5.6.2.3 What's a causal diamond? It's essentially defined by gluing together a forward and backwards lightcone. In more detail, if we have a point p in spacetime and a point q in its future, we consider the future lightcone of p and the backwards lightcone of q. These meet at a spacelike surface S; the causal diamond is the union of the interiors of the forward and backwards lightcone up until S.

2.5.6.2.4 Any finite experiment carried out by an observer lives in some causal diamond. Why is this? If we consider an observer who evolves from a point p in spacetime to a later point q, any effect the observer can have, for instance setting up a measurement device, lies in the future lightcone of p. And any information that they can observe lies in the past lightcone of q. Thus the effects they can observe from a given experiment are determined by the sequence of quantum states inside the diamond.

2.5.6.2.5 This means that the future boundary of the causal diamond(i.e. the part consisting of the backwards lightcone) provides an objective choice of "environment" to condition on when considering the results of experiments performed in the diamond.

  • 2.5.6.2.5.1 Note that conditioning on photon states on the boundary may also decohere events outside of the diamond in its causal past. For example, we can run an experiment on Earth measuring the cosmic microwave background. This is correlated with quantum events in the distant past, but photons leaving our local causal diamond contain enough information to decohere them(due to correlations of our measuring apparatus, brains etc. with the events). A finite diamond will generally not have enough information on its future boundary to decohere all classical-like events in its past, however.

2.5.6.2.6 So this gives us a local objective notion of decoherence. The causal diamond also has the nice feature that it defines a branch-like structure on the set of possible measurement results. We can consider information that has left the future boundary up until a given point. For instance, say we measure a system, wait a bit, then perform further measurements on the same system. The photons associated with the first measurement will leave the causal diamond's future boundary before the photons associated with the second.


2.5.6.2.7 How do we extend this to a global picture? The idea is to consider an indefinitely long-lived observer, and take the limit of diamonds defined by a sequence of points on their future trajectory. This will produce a sequence of diamonds of unbounded area(in asymptotically flat universes). Some photons will escape the sequence of diamonds -- aka, for any diamond, some time evolution of the photon's state will be on the boundary. We may equivalently say that these photons escape to null infinity(which is simply the space of possible unbounded photon trajectories). Conditioning on these photon states provides a limiting notion of decoherence and branching for the past of the limiting causal diamond.

  • 2.5.6.2.7.1 In what sense is this a global picture? For an indefinitely long-lived observer in an asymptotically flat universe, their past light cone eventually includes every location in their universe[1]. So every location in spacetime is eventually included in the volume that can potentially be decohered by the limiting photons.
  • 2.5.6.2.7.2 This construction doesn't apply to non-asymptotically flat spacetimes. In universes with a positive cosmological constant, observers' past lightcones don't eventually include everything, as accelerating expansion means an increasing volume of spacetime is forever out of their reach. In this case the future boundary of the diamond approaches a cosmic horizon with finite entropy.
  • 2.5.6.2.7.3 Our universe appears to be of this type, with a (very tiny) positive cosmological constant. That said, it's not out of the question that the apparent c.c. is actually time-dependent(due to quintessence say) and decaying to zero. And there are ways to try adapting the construction to non-asymptotically-flat universes.

2.5.6.2.8 The use of the order in which photons escape to define a branching order bears some resemblance to Kent's proposal to define beables via conditioning only on future events outside a point's future lightcone. If we consider an observer evolving forward in time through a Kentian multiverse, they condition on an increasingly large portion of the future surface. This defines a tree-like structure on the set of possible worlds, which seems plausibly equivalent to that defined by Bousso & Susskind's construction in the limit of the future surface approaching infinity.

2.5.6.3 General Discussion

2.5.6.3.1 So that's my preferred family of definitions of wavefunction branches. Why do I like them?

2.5.6.3.2 First of all, they are plausibly correct. That is, it's plausible that, given a quantum state corresponding to our early universe, if you applied the time evolution operator followed by a late-time photon measurement operator, you would in fact get the set of states and probabilities corresponding to what we intuitively think of as quasiclassical worlds. I know of no other proposed definition that seems as likely to me to meet this bar.

2.5.6.3.3 Secondly, they are elegant. The set of worlds is defined by a single measurement, using the standard quantum definition of measurement. The branching structure is determined by a sequence of measurements, themselves determined by geometrically natural constructs from relativity. There are no arbitrary constants.

2.5.6.3.4 "Isn't the retroactive nature of the construct kinda wacky?" Any definition of wavefunction branching will have at least a bit of a retroactive character, because isolated systems can only be said to have decohered/branched some time after their initial interaction with the environment has sufficiently propagated records/increased the complexity.

2.5.6.3.5 Here's a general argument against any definition of wavefunction branching that doesn't rely on some sort of asymptotic late-time measurement. Say we have a definition based on (e.g.) number of copies of records, or circuit complexity. Then it would be possible for a sufficiently technologically advanced civilization to "spoof" the definition by conducting an experiment in which they evolve an isolated quantum system to meet the definition, then reverse the evolution. According to the definition, branches would form and then re-merge! A set of branches in a sensible definition should never do this.

2.5.6.3.6 This concludes my account of the problem of defining wavefunction branches/the measurement problem. Now what does this have to do with our original goal of explaining the relation between the laws of physics and the existence of life/sentience?
